summary: A binary search tree keeps values ordered: every key in a node's left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger. That ordering makes search, insert, and delete take time proportional to the tree's height.

sections.heading: The BST property
bullets: left subtree keys < node key < right subtree keys, recursively.
In-order traversal (left, node, right) visits keys in sorted order.
Duplicates need a policy: reject, count, or place consistently on one side.

sections.heading: Search
sections.body: Compare with the node: go left if smaller, right if larger, stop when equal or NULL. O(h).

sections.heading: Insert
sections.body: Search for the key's position; attach a new leaf where the search ends. O(h).

sections.heading: Delete: three cases
bullets: One child: replace the node with its child.
Two children: copy the in-order successor (minimum of the right subtree) into the node, then delete that successor.

sections.heading: Complexity and shape
sections.body: Height h is between log2(n) (balanced) and n (degenerate). Inserting sorted keys 1, 2, 3, ... builds a linked list and makes every operation O(n). Self-balancing trees keep h = O(log n).

bullets: Inorder: sorted output; also used to validate a BST.
Preorder: root first; used to copy or serialize a tree.
Postorder: children first; used to delete or evaluate.

sections.body: Min is the leftmost node, max the rightmost. Successor is the minimum of the right subtree, or else the nearest ancestor reached from a left child. Floor and ceiling find the closest key at or below or above x.

AVL trees keep subtree heights within 1 using rotations; red-black trees use color rules for looser balance with fewer rotations. Both guarantee O(log n). Standard maps (`std::map`, `TreeMap`) use red-black trees.
Checking only each node against its immediate children is wrong. Pass down allowed (min, max) bounds, or verify that an in-order traversal is strictly increasing.
Hash tables give O(1) average lookup but no ordering. BSTs give O(log n) with range queries, sorted iteration, and nearest-key lookup.

takeaways: Left < node < right, at every node.
Search/insert/delete are O(h): O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed.
Use AVL/red-black trees to guarantee balance.
